description: Gkeyll's C/C++/CUDA code style is enforced by clang-format. Use when writing or editing any .c/.h/.cpp/.hpp/.cu/.cuh file, to know how to format it and which files must never be reformatted.
user-invocable: true
---

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

name: compiling
description: How to compile Gkeyll libraries, executables, and specific unit or regression test targets on CPU or CUDA.
---

# Instructions

Use this skill whenever you need to compile
* Any of the Gkeyll libraries.
* A C unit or regression test.
* A C input file.

# Compiling in Gkeyll

We assume the dependencies have already been installed (e.g. via a machines/mkdeps
file) and configured (e.g. via a machines/configure file).

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).
Dependencies are typically already installed in the sibling `gkylsoft/`
directory. Check the existing configuration before building. If configuration
is missing or needs changing, consult `machines/configure.<machine>.sh` for
required modules and library paths, or use `./configure` with the intended
installation prefix and solver.

## Compiling the Gkeyll library

We compile using a Makefile. The `make` command allows you to specify the number
of cores to use via `-j`. We will use no more than half the available processors for parallel builds.
So before invoking `make`, set the `NPROC` environment variable on a Mac using
```
export NPROC=$(sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu)
NPROC=$((NPROC > 1 ? NPROC / 2 : 1))
```
or on Linux using

```sh
NPROC=$(nproc)
NPROC=$((NPROC > 1 ? NPROC / 2 : 1))
```

Then, you can build the Gkeyll library with

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" install
```

## Compiling a C unit or regression test

Unit tests are located in the `unit/` directory of each solver
(core/moments/vlasov/gyrokinetic/pkpm), while C regression tests are located in `creg/` folders and
have names beginning with `rt_`.

Compile a specific test by giving make its executable target:

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" build/core/unit/ctest_array
make -j"$NPROC" build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

CPU targets are located in `build/`, and  GPU targets are in `cuda-build/`.
Match test targets to the configured build directory.

For executing the resulting tests, see
[testing-and-verification](../testing-and-verification/SKILL.md).

### Compiling all or groups of C unit tests

The Makefile supports compiling groups of unit tests all at once. For example, to compile all the
unit tests at once run

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit
```

Alternatively, you can compile all the unit tests for a specific solver. For example, to compile all
the unit tests for the gyrokinetic solver use

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit
```

## Compiling C input files

Input files written in C work just like C regression tests. They can be compiled similarly if they
are located in the `creg/` folder. For example, if `my_sim.c` is a gyrokinetic input file, and located
in `gyrokinetic/creg/`, it can be compiled with

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" build/gyrokinetic/creg/my_sim
```

If the input file is outside of the repository, use the shared makefile in
`<gkeyll_install_prefix>/share/`. Run it from the directory containing the input
file:

```sh
cd <input_file_directory>
cp <gkeyll_install_prefix>/share/Makefile ./
make
```

name: testing-and-verification
description: How to run and write Gkeyll unit and regression tests, as well as performing memory checks. Use when testing changes and verifying that changes didn't break the code or change simulation results.
---

# Instructions

* Unit tests only test the /zero layer. Regression tests test the /app layer.
* Unit tests are focused on particular /zero modules and bear the same name as the module they test.
  For example, `core/unit/ctest_array.c` tests the `core/zero/array.c` module.
* Unit tests should be modular, test only what is necessary, and be simple.
* Only test code that you understand completely.
* For code changes, run relevant unit tests and focused regression tests when
  simulation behavior is affected. Choose tests based on the changed component.
* Do not run the entire regression suite unless you are asked to; it can take a long time.
  Use the task's scope and available resources to choose the suitable testing scope.
* For documentation or agent configuration changes, validate the changed files
  and references; solver tests and memory checks are unnecessary.
* Report what was checked and any checks that could not run. If required context
  is missing or unreadable, report the exact path rather than silently skipping it.

# Running unit tests

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

In order to run all Gkeyll unit tests:
1. Compile all unit tests; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests with
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit-run
```

In order to run all unit tests for a specific solver, e.g. gyrokinetic:
1. Compile all unit tests for that solver; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests for that solver, e.g. for gyrokinetic use
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit-run
```

One can also compile and run a single unit test of interest. Simply:
1. Compile the unit; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run the executable from the repository root:
For example, in order to run `core/unit/ctest_array.c` do

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

If the Gkeyll was build on a CPU-only machine or without GPU support, unit tests will simply ignore
GPU tests (via pre-processor if-statements). When running on a machine with a supported GPU, and if
Gkeyll is configured to build GPU code, running these tests will automatically run the corresponding
GPU tests. If a GPU is not available but Gkeyll was built to use GPUs, the GPU tests may simply fail
or exit (e.g. due to GPU memory allocation errors).

### Parallel unit tests

There are a few parallel unit tests that use MPI, whose names begin with `mctest`. These tests are
compiled the same way as serial tests, but must be run with the appropriate MPI execution command.

For example if Gkeyll was built and configured with the MPI in `gkylsoft/openmpi/`, then a parallel
unit test (for example `mctest_mpi_comm.c`) may be run with

```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 4 build/core/unit/mctest_mpi_comm
```

# Running regression tests

## C regression tests

Regression tests written in C and located in `creg/` directories need to be compiled first,
see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).

Once compiled the regression test may be run serially with, for
`gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1.c` for example:
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

See 
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -h
```
for command line arguments that may be available (not all are actually supported). For
example, the following command
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -s1
```
limits the regression to a one-step smoke test.

CUDA builds place the executable in `cuda-build/` instead of `build/`, and regression tests use `-g`
to indicate GPU execution.

## Parallel regression tests

Regression executables take the `-M` command line argument to indicate a parallel run (requiring
MPI). The flags `-c X -d Y -e Z` specify that the first, second and third configuration-space
dimensions are to be subdivided amongs X, Y and Z MPI processes, respecitively. The product `X*Y*Z`
must match the number of cores available for this run. If one of `-c`, `-d` or `-e` is not given,
it is assumed to be 1.

For example, we may run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 cores in the second
dimension with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -M -d 2
```

For gyrokinetic partition restrictions and an example, read
[gyrokinetic-details](../gyrokinetic-details/SKILL.md).

It is also possible to run with multiple GPUs. Gkeyll's model is to match each MPI process to a
single GPU. The procedure is similar as for multiple GPUs, but the additional `-g` flag is needed.
For example, to run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 GPUs in the second dimension
with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -g -M -d 2
```

## Lua regression tests

Run Lua inputs using the installed executable:

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll <Lua_input_file>
```

## The runregression tool

After installing the Gkeyll library and executable one may use the `runregression` tool to run
regression tests, see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll runregression -h
```

After configuring runregression, and having generated accepted results with
`runregression run create`, one may check the test using `runregression run check`. Note that the
flag `-r` allows check a specific test or set of tests.

The runregression tool produces SQL databases that may be examined with the `queryrdb` command,
see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll queryrdb -h
```

# Memory checks

All code must be free of memory errors and leaks. Run the relevant CPU test
under Valgrind before committing:

```sh
valgrind --leak-check=full ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

For GPU changes, run the relevant executable under Compute Sanitizer:

```sh
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --leak-check full <executable>
```

Supply the executable's GPU options where required. Report unavailable tools
or hardware and distinguish completed checks from checks that could not run.

# Gkeyll CI system

Gkeyll has a CI system based on Jenkins which calls the aforementioned existing functionality to run
unit and regression tests. See ci/jenkins/README.md for more details.

In the gyrokinetic solver gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_lapd_cyl_3x2v_p1.c uses a cylindrical mapping in mapc2p, with a minimum radius (currently (2.5 * ctx.rho_s)) to avoid placing the innermost radial boundary at r=0 where some geometric quantities may diverge. I'm interested in going down to r=0, however. I've noticed that when I set the minimum radius to 0 some of the geometric quantities gxxj, gxyj or gyyj diverge, but I don't think they should. I think this may because the mapc2p program flow first divides by radius and later multiples by radius, or viceversa.

Would it be possible to create a separate geometry object, like gyrokinetic/zero/gk_geometry_mapc2p.c, solely for cylindrical coordinates that allows one to go down to r=0?
Implement the plan.

- How the geometric quantities at the axis are discretized.
- How the field solver handls the axis.
- How the collisionless terms handle the lower radial boundary.
Regarding the first finding: would it be sufficient to change gkyl_gk_collisionless_flux so that if the BC is zero flux, it selects a kernel that sets the flux to zero?

---
name: testing-and-verification
description: How to run and write Gkeyll unit and regression tests, as well as performing memory checks. Use when testing changes and verifying that changes didn't break the code or change simulation results.
---

# Instructions

* Unit tests only test the /zero layer. Regression tests test the /app layer.
* Unit tests are focused on particular /zero modules and bear the same name as the module they test.
  For example, `core/unit/ctest_array.c` tests the `core/zero/array.c` module.
* Unit tests should be modular, test only what is necessary, and be simple.
* Only test code that you understand completely.
* For code changes, run relevant unit tests and focused regression tests when
  simulation behavior is affected. Choose tests based on the changed component.
* Do not run the entire regression suite unless you are asked to; it can take a long time.
  Use the task's scope and available resources to choose the suitable testing scope.
* For documentation or agent configuration changes, validate the changed files
  and references; solver tests and memory checks are unnecessary.
* Report what was checked and any checks that could not run. If required context
  is missing or unreadable, report the exact path rather than silently skipping it.

# Running unit tests

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

In order to run all Gkeyll unit tests:
1. Compile all unit tests; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests with
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit-run
```

In order to run all unit tests for a specific solver, e.g. gyrokinetic:
1. Compile all unit tests for that solver; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run all unit tests for that solver, e.g. for gyrokinetic use
```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit-run
```

One can also compile and run a single unit test of interest. Simply:
1. Compile the unit; see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).
2. Run the executable from the repository root:
For example, in order to run `core/unit/ctest_array.c` do

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

If the Gkeyll was build on a CPU-only machine or without GPU support, unit tests will simply ignore
GPU tests (via pre-processor if-statements). When running on a machine with a supported GPU, and if
Gkeyll is configured to build GPU code, running these tests will automatically run the corresponding
GPU tests. If a GPU is not available but Gkeyll was built to use GPUs, the GPU tests may simply fail
or exit (e.g. due to GPU memory allocation errors).

### Parallel unit tests

There are a few parallel unit tests that use MPI, whose names begin with `mctest`. These tests are
compiled the same way as serial tests, but must be run with the appropriate MPI execution command.

For example if Gkeyll was built and configured with the MPI in `gkylsoft/openmpi/`, then a parallel
unit test (for example `mctest_mpi_comm.c`) may be run with

```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 4 build/core/unit/mctest_mpi_comm
```

# Running regression tests

## C regression tests

Regression tests written in C and located in `creg/` directories need to be compiled first,
see [compilation](../compiling/SKILL.md).

Once compiled the regression test may be run serially with, for
`gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1.c` for example:
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

See 
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -h
```
for command line arguments that may be available (not all are actually supported). For
example, the following command
```sh
./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -s1
```
limits the regression to a one-step smoke test.

CUDA builds place the executable in `cuda-build/` instead of `build/`, and regression tests use `-g`
to indicate GPU execution.

## Parallel regression tests

Regression executables take the `-M` command line argument to indicate a parallel run (requiring
MPI). The flags `-c X -d Y -e Z` specify that the first, second and third configuration-space
dimensions are to be subdivided amongs X, Y and Z MPI processes, respecitively. The product `X*Y*Z`
must match the number of cores available for this run. If one of `-c`, `-d` or `-e` is not given,
it is assumed to be 1.

For example, we may run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 cores in the second
dimension with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -M -d 2
```

For gyrokinetic partition restrictions and an example, read
[gyrokinetic-details](../gyrokinetic-details/SKILL.md).

It is also possible to run with multiple GPUs. Gkeyll's model is to match each MPI process to a
single GPU. The procedure is similar as for multiple GPUs, but the additional `-g` flag is needed.
For example, to run `gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1` using 2 GPUs in the second dimension
with
```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 2 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -g -M -d 2
```

## Lua regression tests

Run Lua inputs using the installed executable:

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll <Lua_input_file>
```

## The runregression tool

After installing the Gkeyll library and executable one may use the `runregression` tool to run
regression tests, see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll runregression -h
```

After configuring runregression, and having generated accepted results with
`runregression run create`, one may check the test using `runregression run check`. Note that the
flag `-r` allows check a specific test or set of tests.

The runregression tool produces SQL databases that may be examined with the `queryrdb` command,
see

```sh
<gkeyll_install_prefix>/bin/gkeyll queryrdb -h
```

# Memory checks

All code must be free of memory errors and leaks. Run the relevant CPU test
under Valgrind before committing:

```sh
valgrind --leak-check=full ./build/core/unit/ctest_array
```

For GPU changes, run the relevant executable under Compute Sanitizer:

```sh
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --leak-check full <executable>
```

Supply the executable's GPU options where required. Report unavailable tools
or hardware and distinguish completed checks from checks that could not run.

# Gkeyll CI system

Gkeyll has a CI system based on Jenkins which calls the aforementioned existing functionality to run
unit and regression tests. See ci/jenkins/README.md for more details.
---
name: compiling
description: How to compile Gkeyll libraries, executables, and specific unit or regression test targets on CPU or CUDA.
---

# Instructions

Use this skill whenever you need to compile
* Any of the Gkeyll libraries.
* A C unit or regression test.
* A C input file.

# Compiling in Gkeyll

We assume the dependencies have already been installed (e.g. via a machines/mkdeps
file) and configured (e.g. via a machines/configure file).

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).
Dependencies are typically already installed in the sibling `gkylsoft/`
directory. Check the existing configuration before building. If configuration
is missing or needs changing, consult `machines/configure.<machine>.sh` for
required modules and library paths, or use `./configure` with the intended
installation prefix and solver.

## Compiling the Gkeyll library

We compile using a Makefile. The `make` command allows you to specify the number
of cores to use via `-j`. We will use no more than half the available processors for parallel builds.
So before invoking `make`, set the `NPROC` environment variable on a Mac using
```
export NPROC=$(sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu)
NPROC=$((NPROC > 1 ? NPROC / 2 : 1))
```
or on Linux using

```sh
NPROC=$(nproc)
NPROC=$((NPROC > 1 ? NPROC / 2 : 1))
```

Then, you can build the Gkeyll library with

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" install
```

## Compiling a C unit or regression test

Unit tests are located in the `unit/` directory of each solver
(core/moments/vlasov/gyrokinetic/pkpm), while C regression tests are located in `creg/` folders and
have names beginning with `rt_`.

Compile a specific test by giving make its executable target:

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" build/core/unit/ctest_array
make -j"$NPROC" build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

CPU targets are located in `build/`, and  GPU targets are in `cuda-build/`.
Match test targets to the configured build directory.

For executing the resulting tests, see
[testing-and-verification](../testing-and-verification/SKILL.md).

### Compiling all or groups of C unit tests

The Makefile supports compiling groups of unit tests all at once. For example, to compile all the
unit tests at once run

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit
```

Alternatively, you can compile all the unit tests for a specific solver. For example, to compile all
the unit tests for the gyrokinetic solver use

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit
```

## Compiling C input files

Input files written in C work just like C regression tests. They can be compiled similarly if they
are located in the `creg/` folder. For example, if `my_sim.c` is a gyrokinetic input file, and located
in `gyrokinetic/creg/`, it can be compiled with

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" build/gyrokinetic/creg/my_sim
```

If the input file is outside of the repository, use the shared makefile in
`<gkeyll_install_prefix>/share/`. Run it from the directory containing the input
file:

```sh
cd <input_file_directory>
cp <gkeyll_install_prefix>/share/Makefile ./
make
```
---
name: code_style
description: Gkeyll's C/C++/CUDA code style is enforced by clang-format. Use when writing or editing any .c/.h/.cpp/.hpp/.cu/.cuh file, to know how to format it and which files must never be reformatted.
user-invocable: true
---

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

Supply the executable's GPU options where required. Report unavailable tools
or hardware and distinguish completed checks from checks that could not run.

Gkeyll has a CI system based on Jenkins which calls the aforementioned existing functionality to run
unit and regression tests. See ci/jenkins/README.md for more details.

name: compiling
description: How to compile Gkeyll libraries, executables, and specific unit or regression test targets on CPU or CUDA.
---

# Instructions

Use this skill whenever you need to compile
* Any of the Gkeyll libraries.
* A C unit or regression test.
* A C input file.

# Compiling in Gkeyll

We assume the dependencies have already been installed (e.g. via a machines/mkdeps
file) and configured (e.g. via a machines/configure file).

Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).
Dependencies are typically already installed in the sibling `gkylsoft/`
directory. Check the existing configuration before building. If configuration
is missing or needs changing, consult `machines/configure.<machine>.sh` for
required modules and library paths, or use `./configure` with the intended
installation prefix and solver.

## Compiling the Gkeyll library

We compile using a Makefile. The `make` command allows you to specify the number
of cores to use via `-j`. We will use no more than half the available processors for parallel builds.
So before invoking `make`, set the `NPROC` environment variable on a Mac using
```
export NPROC=$(sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu)
NPROC=$((NPROC > 1 ? NPROC / 2 : 1))
```
or on Linux using

```sh
NPROC=$(nproc)
NPROC=$((NPROC > 1 ? NPROC / 2 : 1))
```

Then, you can build the Gkeyll library with

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" install
```

## Compiling a C unit or regression test

Unit tests are located in the `unit/` directory of each solver
(core/moments/vlasov/gyrokinetic/pkpm), while C regression tests are located in `creg/` folders and
have names beginning with `rt_`.

Compile a specific test by giving make its executable target:

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" build/core/unit/ctest_array
make -j"$NPROC" build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
```

CPU targets are located in `build/`, and  GPU targets are in `cuda-build/`.
Match test targets to the configured build directory.

For executing the resulting tests, see
[testing-and-verification](../testing-and-verification/SKILL.md).

### Compiling all or groups of C unit tests

The Makefile supports compiling groups of unit tests all at once. For example, to compile all the
unit tests at once run

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" unit
```

Alternatively, you can compile all the unit tests for a specific solver. For example, to compile all
the unit tests for the gyrokinetic solver use

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" gyrokinetic-unit
```

## Compiling C input files

Input files written in C work just like C regression tests. They can be compiled similarly if they
are located in the `creg/` folder. For example, if `my_sim.c` is a gyrokinetic input file, and located
in `gyrokinetic/creg/`, it can be compiled with

```sh
make -j"$NPROC" build/gyrokinetic/creg/my_sim
```

If the input file is outside of the repository, use the shared makefile in
`<gkeyll_install_prefix>/share/`. Run it from the directory containing the input
file:

```sh
cd <input_file_directory>
cp <gkeyll_install_prefix>/share/Makefile ./
make
```

name: code_style
description: Gkeyll's C/C++/CUDA code style is enforced by clang-format. Use when writing or editing any .c/.h/.cpp/.hpp/.cu/.cuh file, to know how to format it and which files must never be reformatted.
user-invocable: true

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

name: software-design
description: Some design practices in Gkeyll code to consider when implementing new modules (apps, updaters) or modifying existing ones.
---

# Instructions

* Load this skill whenever new modules or updaters in zero/ or apps/ folders
  are to be created, or when existing ones will be edited.

## Software design elements

### Module structure

Most modules in zero/ or apps/ consist of 3 public functions:
1. A creation function, typically called gkyl_<module>_new or gkyl_<module>_init.
2. An execution function, often called gkyl_<module>_advance or gkyl_<module>_apply.
3. A deletion function, typically called gkyl_<module>_release.

There may also be some additional auxiliary private or public functions.

### Module best practices

- All dynamic (heap) allocations should happen in the initialization function,
  and freed in the release function, using the appropriate gkyl_ allocation/deallocation functions when possible.
- Don't place logic branching (e.g. if-statements) that depend on a
  time-independent choice or parameter inside the methods called in the time loop of a simulation
  (e.g. _advance). Instead, use function pointers to set the appropriate method during the initialization
  of the module, and call that method inside the time loop.
- Function signatures in header files should contain a brief comment describing
  what the function does, and a description of each argument following existing styles.
- Methods to initialize an updater in zero/ which take all arguments inside a
  single input struct should have a name with the suffix _inew (instead of _new).

### Other principles to follow

- Consider extensibility, maintainability, simplicity and how modular design.
- Avoid code duplication whenever possible (e.g. write functions called
  multiple times) and without breaking layering.
- Write shorter code and refactor into a sub-module whenever possible.

name: software-design
description: Some design practices in Gkeyll code to consider when implementing new modules (apps, updaters) or modifying existing ones.
---

# Instructions

* Load this skill whenever new modules or updaters in zero/ or apps/ folders
  are to be created, or when existing ones will be edited.

## Software design elements

### Module structure

Most modules in zero/ or apps/ consist of 3 public functions:
1. A creation function, typically called gkyl_<module>_new or gkyl_<module>_init.
2. An execution function, often called gkyl_<module>_advance or gkyl_<module>_apply.
3. A deletion function, typically called gkyl_<module>_release.

There may also be some additional auxiliary private or public functions.

### Module best practices

- All dynamic (heap) allocations should happen in the initialization function,
  and freed in the release function, using the appropriate gkyl_ allocation/deallocation functions when possible.
- Don't place logic branching (e.g. if-statements) that depend on a
  time-independent choice or parameter inside the methods called in the time loop of a simulation
  (e.g. _advance). Instead, use function pointers to set the appropriate method during the initialization
  of the module, and call that method inside the time loop.
- Function signatures in header files should contain a brief comment describing
  what the function does, and a description of each argument following existing styles.
- Methods to initialize an updater in zero/ which take all arguments inside a
  single input struct should have a name with the suffix _inew (instead of _new).

### Other principles to follow

- Consider extensibility, maintainability, simplicity and how modular design.
- Avoid code duplication whenever possible (e.g. write functions called
  multiple times) and without breaking layering.
- Write shorter code and refactor into a sub-module whenever possible.

# Cylindrical geometry and axis treatment: implementation and review

Reviewed on 2026-10-20 against the current working-tree changes. This document
describes the implementation as it exists, including defects found during the
review. No solver source was changed as part of this review.

The analytic cylindrical geometry and the constrained perpendicular field solve
are a useful foundation. However, the collisionless surface-flux evaluation still
executes a singular kernel at the axis. The passing geometry/Poisson unit tests
and the previously reported short LAPD run do not establish that the complete
axis implementation is correct.

## 1. Review findings

### R1 — High priority: the axis flux kernel still divides by zero

**Location:** `apps/gk_species_collisionless.c:284–289`, with the downstream
selection in `zero/gkyl_gk_collisionless_flux_priv.h:318` and execution in
`zero/gk_collisionless_flux.c:154`.

The new code translates `GKYL_BC_GK_SPECIES_AXIS` into
`GKYL_BC_GK_SPECIES_ZERO_FLUX` for the surface-flux updater. That updater's kernel
selector distinguishes `GKYL_BC_GK_SKIP` from the other boundary types; it does
not give `ZERO_FLUX` a no-op or zero-flux kernel. Consequently, the lower radial
face still calls `gk_collisionless_flux_surfx_3x2v_ser_p1`.

At the axis, the new geometry supplies `Jc=0` and `area_elem=0`. The selected
kernel computes expressions containing both `1/area_elem` and `area_elem/Jc`.
For example, its electrostatic drift contribution has the structure

```text
alpha = (... + [b_theta*d_z H - b_z*d_theta H]/(q*B*area_elem))
        * area_elem/Jc
```

This produces undefined arithmetic before the DG RHS updater applies its
zero-flux boundary treatment. A direct call to the linked kernel with constant
potential, positive constant axial B, and the axis geometry produced:

```text
axis: nonfinite radial flux slots = 24/24, cfl = 0
r=1 control: nonfinite radial flux slots = 0/24, cfl = 0
```

The zero CFL in this check is not proof of a valid calculation: `fmax` can hide
NaNs while the flux array still contains them. The RHS boundary kernel omits
the axis flux, which explains how a short simulation can finish despite this
defect. Flux diagnostics can nevertheless contain NaNs, and the invalid
arithmetic remains dependent on compiler and floating-point behavior.

**Recommended correction:** give the axis an explicit surface-flux path that
writes the radial flux slots to zero and returns zero boundary CFL before any
division by the Jacobian or face area. Implement the equivalent behavior on CPU
and CUDA, and audit the passive-advection path as well. Continue using the RHS
boundary kernel that retains the interior face contribution. Do not rely on
the zero sentinel stored in `jacobtot_inv_nodal`: this flux kernel obtains `Jc`
directly from the DG geometry and performs its own divisions.

### R2 — Medium priority: parallel position maps silently create inconsistent geometry

**Location:** `zero/gk_geometry_cylindrical.c:68–80`.

The constructor delegates coordinate sampling to mapc2p, which applies the
position map in all three directions. The cylindrical override checks only
the mapped X and Y coordinates against the unmodified cylindrical map. It
does not check mapped Z, and then hard-codes the z tangent, dual, metric, and
Jacobian for an identity z map.

A direct constructor check with a constant axial magnetic field and
`position_map->maps[2]` set to `z -> 2*z` succeeded and reported:

```text
z -> 2z accepted: g_zz = 1 (expected 4), J/r = 1 (expected 2)
```

The stored physical coordinates and metric therefore describe different maps.
Parallel streaming, volume weights, and field coefficients would be incorrect
for such an input.

**Recommended correction:** explicitly reject nonidentity position maps in
all three directions for the initial implementation, or include their
derivatives consistently in every analytic quantity. Merely checking mapped
values at a few quadrature points is not a general derivative check.

### R3 — Medium priority: cylindrical field initialization drops bias lines

**Location:** `apps/gk_field_2x3x.c:665–671` and
`zero/fem_poisson_perp.c:625`.

The existing constructor receives `f->info.bias_line_list`. The new cylindrical
constructor has no bias-line parameter and passes a null list to the shared
implementation. Thus a cylindrical input specifying bias lines silently loses
those perpendicular field constraints. The assertion inside the shared
constructor cannot detect this, because it receives the null pointer supplied
by the wrapper rather than the user's list.

**Recommended correction:** reject a nonempty list at the app call site until
it is supported, or pass the list through and define how a constraint touching
the axis interacts with the collapsed nodes.

**Location:** `apps/gk_species_collisionless.c:284–289`, with the downstream
selection in `zero/gkyl_gk_collisionless_flux_priv.h:318` and execution in
`zero/gk_collisionless_flux.c:154`.

The new code translates `GKYL_BC_GK_SPECIES_AXIS` into
`GKYL_BC_GK_SPECIES_ZERO_FLUX` for the surface-flux updater. That updater's kernel
selector distinguishes `GKYL_BC_GK_SKIP` from the other boundary types; it does
not give `ZERO_FLUX` a no-op or zero-flux kernel. Consequently, the lower radial
face still calls `gk_collisionless_flux_surfx_3x2v_ser_p1`.

At the axis, the new geometry supplies `Jc=0` and `area_elem=0`. The selected
kernel computes expressions containing both `1/area_elem` and `area_elem/Jc`.
For example, its electrostatic drift contribution has the structure

```text
alpha = (... + [b_theta*d_z H - b_z*d_theta H]/(q*B*area_elem))
        * area_elem/Jc
```

This produces undefined arithmetic before the DG RHS updater applies its
zero-flux boundary treatment. A direct call to the linked kernel with constant
potential, positive constant axial B, and the axis geometry produced:

```text
axis: nonfinite radial flux slots = 24/24, cfl = 0
r=1 control: nonfinite radial flux slots = 0/24, cfl = 0
```

The zero CFL in this check is not proof of a valid calculation: `fmax` can hide
NaNs while the flux array still contains them. The RHS boundary kernel omits
the axis flux, which explains how a short simulation can finish despite this
defect. Flux diagnostics can nevertheless contain NaNs, and the invalid
arithmetic remains dependent on compiler and floating-point behavior.

**Recommended correction:** give the axis an explicit surface-flux path that
writes the radial flux slots to zero and returns zero boundary CFL before any
division by the Jacobian or face area. Implement the equivalent behavior on CPU
and CUDA, and audit the passive-advection path as well. Continue using the RHS
boundary kernel that retains the interior face contribution. Do not rely on
the zero sentinel stored in `jacobtot_inv_nodal`: this flux kernel obtains `Jc`
directly from the DG geometry and performs its own divisions.

### R2 — Medium priority: parallel position maps silently create inconsistent geometry

**Location:** `zero/gk_geometry_cylindrical.c:68–80`.

The constructor delegates coordinate sampling to mapc2p, which applies the
position map in all three directions. The cylindrical override checks only
the mapped X and Y coordinates against the unmodified cylindrical map. It
does not check mapped Z, and then hard-codes the z tangent, dual, metric, and
Jacobian for an identity z map.

A direct constructor check with a constant axial magnetic field and
`position_map->maps[2]` set to `z -> 2*z` succeeded and reported:

```text

```

The stored physical coordinates and metric therefore describe different maps.
Parallel streaming, volume weights, and field coefficients would be incorrect
for such an input.

**Recommended correction:** explicitly reject nonidentity position maps in
all three directions for the initial implementation, or include their
derivatives consistently in every analytic quantity. Merely checking mapped
values at a few quadrature points is not a general derivative check.

### R3 — Medium priority: cylindrical field initialization drops bias lines

**Location:** `apps/gk_field_2x3x.c:665–671` and
`zero/fem_poisson_perp.c:625`.

The existing constructor receives `f->info.bias_line_list`. The new cylindrical

The full local angular ring and an even number of angular cells make the
half-turn an exact cell permutation. A decomposed angular ring would require
communication that is absent here. Periodic synchronization occurs before the
physical BC loop; ordinary communicator synchronization follows it.

### 6.2 DG RHS boundary treatment

The app marks the lower radial direction as zero flux when constructing the
collisionless DG updater. In `vlasov/zero/hyper_dg.c`, this selects
`boundary_surf_term` for the first radial cell. That boundary update retains
the flux on the other, interior radial face and omits the external axis-face
contribution. The volume term is still evaluated at positive interior Gauss
nodes, and theta/z/velocity transport remains active.

Physically, for regular fields and a bounded distribution, the radial
integrated flux through a cylinder of radius r vanishes as its area shrinks
to zero. A zero axis boundary contribution is therefore appropriate. The
opposite-angle ghost fill does not supply an additional transport flux through
the collapsed point.

### 6.3 Surface-flux preprocessing is a separate step

Before the DG RHS update, `gk_species_collisionless_rhs_enabled` calls the
surface-flux updater. That updater computes the lower face for every interior
cell, including the first radial cell. As described in R1, mapping the enum
to `ZERO_FLUX` does not suppress this calculation.

The current behavior is therefore:

1. Fill opposite-angle ghosts.
2. Evaluate an ordinary radial surface kernel at r=0, reading those ghosts
   and generating invalid flux values.
3. Use the zero-flux RHS boundary kernel, which does not consume that axis
   flux in the radial RHS contribution.

This is different from explicitly setting the axis flux to zero. It is also
why the source comment claiming that the axis boundary updater never samples
the undefined geometry is too broad. The modal inverse sentinel itself is
not used by this kernel, but the singular Jacobian/area data are.

## 7. Simplicity, modularity, maintainability, and performance

The changes have several useful properties: enum values are appended, generic
geometry behavior is selected explicitly, existing generated FEM kernels are
reused, the node constraint is small and inspectable, and the field fallback
has clear allocation/release ownership. The original annular regression is
also preserved in the current tree.

The principal design improvements I recommend after fixing R1–R3 are:

- **Separate analytic sampling from finite-difference sampling.** The new
  object currently delegates to mapc2p, which still constructs finite-
  difference samples before dispatching to the analytic formulas. Reuse common
  allocation/projection helpers, but avoid computing unused derivative data
  for a known analytic map. This is primarily initialization cost.
- **Make the axis BC a zero-layer updater.** The array permutation and modal
  reflection are independently testable numerical operations. Keeping them
  in a small updater would simplify CPU/CUDA ownership and avoid the large
  allocation inside the app time loop identified in R4.
- **Select the field execution function during initialization.** The geometry
  type and device choice do not change during a run. A function pointer for
  the host-staged solve follows the repository design convention and avoids
  redispatching on those choices in every RHS call. The branch cost itself
  is minor compared with the transfers and solve.
- **Document and centralize the p1 node ordering.** The indices 0,2,4,6 and
  lookup-kernel index 2 are valid assumptions that deserve named helpers or
  explicit comments. Reusing the already allocated kernel table would also
  remove the temporary allocate/free/reallocate sequence in the constructor.
- **Keep the retained unused Poisson slots initially.** Compacting them would
  save `2*(Ntheta-1)` slots per parallel-cell problem, but requires more
  numbering logic. Their isolated identity rows are a reasonable simplicity
  tradeoff until profiling establishes a meaningful cost.
- **Clarify the public contract.** Document positive axial B, identity
  position maps, full angular coverage, even angular resolution, p1, CPU
  Poisson execution, and required species/field BCs. Add initialization
  checks for unsupported combinations rather than relying on an eventual
  assertion during a BC application. Current assertions also disappear in
  builds defining `NDEBUG`.
- **Reduce duplication in analytic formulas.** Interior and surface routines
  repeat tangent, dual, normal, and metric assignments. A small helper with
  an explicit axis case would make their consistency easier to maintain.
  The projection macro also hides repeated full nodal-range traversals;
  computing related fields together would be clearer. These are secondary
  concerns relative to the time-loop GPU copies.

## 8. Verification performed and remaining gaps

The following existing executables were run during this review and passed:

```text
build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gk_geometry_cylindrical
build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_fem_poisson_perp_cylindrical
build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_gk_geometry_mapc2p
build/gyrokinetic/unit/ctest_fem_poisson_perp
```

The changed library sources were older than the linked library, and the new
unit-test sources were older than their executables. Two additional temporary
C probes linked against that library reproduced R1 and R2. They were compiled
without `-ffast-math`, so their finite-value checks were not optimized away.
The kernel itself was the existing compiled library implementation.

The geometry unit test checks selected coefficients for finiteness using
bit inspection, which is appropriate for the library's fast-math build. It
does not test the collisionless surface updater. The field test checks
single-valued axis potential and decreasing error on two meshes for

\[
\phi=(1-r^2)/4,\quad \rho=r,
\]

and

\[
\phi=(r-r^3)\cos\theta,\quad \rho=8r^2\cos\theta.
\]

These source expressions include the radial Jacobian appropriate to the weak
equation. The field test constructs epsilon itself instead of obtaining it
from the new geometry object, so the geometry-to-field interface is not
tested end to end. It measures error at cell centers and only requires the
fine-grid error to be smaller, rather than checking a convergence rate.

The previously reported ten-step LAPD run is a smoke test. Its density
callback restarts a fixed-seed RNG on each call, making the nominal random
perturbation the same each time; it does not provide a controlled angular
transport test. A successful exit cannot detect the hidden flux NaNs above.

The next focused checks should be an app or flux-updater test asserting
finite flux/CFL/RHS arrays and exactly zero radial axis flux; a regular angular
mode transported near/across the origin with conservation checks; rejection
of unsupported maps and bias lines; and an end-to-end manufactured field solve
using the cylindrical geometry coefficients. GPU parity and boundary memory
checks should accompany the device implementation.

CUDA execution, Compute Sanitizer, and Valgrind were unavailable in this review
environment. MPI execution was not tested during this review. No claim of
GPU or MPI verification is made here.

item.stdout:
Surface geometry uses a face location in the normal direction and Gauss nodes
in the tangential directions. Thus the lower radial surface samples r=0,
whereas theta and z surfaces use positive interior radial nodes.

The surface routine sets the exact Jacobian and face area factors:

\[
J=r,\qquad
\mathtt{lenr}=\begin{cases}r&\text{radial face},\\1&\text{angular face},\\r&\text{axial face}.\end{cases}
\]

At the radial axis face, `jacobgeo_nodal`, `cmag_nodal`, and `lenr_nodal` are
zero. The undefined angular dual, its magnitude, and `jacobtot_inv_nodal` are
assigned zero sentinels instead of evaluating 1/r. The radial unit normal is
still stored using the angular label; it is a directional limiting vector,
not a unique normal to the collapsed physical point.

The existing surface-expansion routine converts these nodal data to surface
modal arrays. `gkyl_gk_dg_geom_populate_surf` also copies the zero Jacobian and
zero face area into `gkdgs.Jc` and `dgs.area_elem`. That second data path is why
the inverse sentinel does not prevent R1.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('gyrokinetic/CYLINDRICAL_AXIS_REVIEW.md')
s=p.read_text()
start=s.index('Reviewed on ')
end=s.index('## 1. Review findings')
s=s[:start]+'''Reviewed on 2026-10-20, with a same-day implementation follow-up for R1.
Sections 2–5 describe the cylindrical geometry and field solver. Section 6
describes the current collisionless axis treatment; section 9 documents the
new Maxima-generated zero-flux kernels, dispatch, regeneration, and tests.

**Current status:** R1 is fixed by selecting explicit zero-flux surface kernels.
The original R1 evidence below records the defect before that fix. R2–R4 remain
open; this follow-up does not change the geometry, field solver, or ghost fill.
Passing the focused tests does not establish convergence or conservation of
the complete axis implementation.

| `ms-gk_collisionless_flux-zero.mac` | Entry point generating all 14 C kernels. |
| `ms-gk_collisionless_flux-zero-header.mac` | Entry point generating the common declaration header. |

The common variant list contains seven direction/layout combinations for
each of two signatures: ES and passive. `ES_NO_BY` shares the ES signature
and kernels. Lower and upper faces also share a kernel: zero flux has no
upwind choice, orientation sign, or dependency on which adjacent cell is skin.
The passive signature retains its two speed inputs even though they are
unused, so it fits the existing updater function-pointer type.

The generated artifacts are copied unchanged into Gkeyll:

- Seven `gk_collisionless_flux_zero_flux_surf*.c` files and
  `gkyl_gk_collisionless_zero_flux_kernels.h` in `ker/gk_collisionless_flux/`.
- Seven `gk_collisionless_passive_flux_zero_flux_surf*.c` files in
  `ker/gk_collisionless_passive_flux/`.

The build discovers these files through the existing kernel-directory rules.
No new build rule or public updater API is required. Generated files must be
regenerated from Maxima rather than edited or formatted by hand.

### 9.2 Discrete flux layout and axis behavior

The generator calls `loadGkBasis`, removes the face-normal configuration
coordinate, and calls `gaussOrdGkHyb` on the remaining configuration and
velocity variables. Thus the number of assignments is derived from the same
hybrid quadrature layout used by the ordinary flux kernels, with three
parallel-velocity nodes and two nodes in each remaining p1 direction.

| Layout | Flux entries per configuration face | Direction block offsets |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| 1x1v p1 | 3 | x: 0 |
| 1x2v p1 | 6 | x: 0 |
| 2x2v p1 | 12 | x: 0, y: 12 |
| 3x2v p1 | 24 | x: 0, y: 24, z: 48 |

For zero-based direction `d` and face count `N`, a kernel assigns precisely
`flux_surf[d*N ... (d+1)*N-1] = 0.0` and returns `0.0`. These are nodal face
flux slots. Other direction blocks and the parallel-velocity block are not
overwritten. For the 3x2v axis this zeros slots 0–23; slots 24–71 and the
parallel-velocity slots starting at 72 retain their normal meaning.

No geometric limit is numerically approximated in this kernel. It imposes the
specified zero numerical boundary flux directly. This is compatible with the
vanishing integrated radial flux of regular fields/distributions at the
collapsed cylindrical face. It does not regularize every cylindrical metric,
change the interior Gauss discretization of `1/r`, or impose additional
regularity on the distribution. The field solver's single-valued axis
potential constraint and the geometry discretization remain as described in
sections 3–5.

### 9.3 Dispatch and performance

The two private flux headers include the new generated header and add small
`GKYL_CU_D` function tables indexed by direction and configuration/velocity
layout. Four ES selectors (lower/upper, ES/NO_BY) and two passive selectors
(lower/upper) handle `ZERO_FLUX` before the existing `SKIP` and normal cases.
Unsupported polynomial orders return null, consistent with the existing
kernel tables. The supported scope remains p1.

CPU constructors and CUDA initialization kernels already call these shared
selectors, so both acquire the new function pointers during initialization.
Interior ES kernels are selected using the existing `ABSORB` selector argument;
interior passive kernels use their existing independent selector. Comments
at the ES constructor call sites now describe this explicitly.

The time loop gains no new BC branch or allocation. Each zero-flux call does
3, 6, 12, or 24 stores plus a zero return, replacing a much larger geometry and
upwind-flux calculation. CUDA source functions carry `GKYL_CU_DH`; the tables
retain the existing device declaration convention. CUDA compilation and
execution still require verification on a CUDA machine.

### 9.4 Regeneration

From the **gkylcas root**, choose an existing output directory and run:

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/gk-zero-flux
maxima --very-quiet --batch-string='gk_zero_flux_out_dir:"/tmp/gk-zero-flux"$ load("gyrokinetic/gk_collisionless/ms-gk_collisionless_flux-zero.mac")$ load("gyrokinetic/gk_collisionless/ms-gk_collisionless_flux-zero-header.mac")$'
cp /tmp/gk-zero-flux/gk_collisionless_flux_zero_flux_*.c ../gkeyll/gyrokinetic/ker/gk_collisionless_flux/
cp /tmp/gk-zero-flux/gkyl_gk_collisionless_zero_flux_kernels.h ../gkeyll/gyrokinetic/ker/gk_collisionless_flux/
cp /tmp/gk-zero-flux/gk_collisionless_passive_flux_zero_flux_*.c ../gkeyll/gyrokinetic/ker/gk_collisionless_passive_flux/
```

Each entry point defaults to `~/max-out` if `gk_zero_flux_out_dir` is unset.
That directory must exist. Inspect Maxima's output for errors as well as
checking the exit status. Two independent generations were compared byte for
byte, and all 15 generated files matched both each other and the Gkeyll copies.

### 9.5 Verification of the fix

New tests:

- `unit/ctest_gk_collisionless_flux.c`: all four layouts, every direction,
  lower and upper ES/NO_BY selectors, and public ES/NO_BY updater tests.
- `unit/ctest_gk_collisionless_passive_flux.c`: the corresponding passive
  selectors and public updater test.
- `unit/gk_collisionless_flux_test.h`: shared 3x2v geometry/array fixture.

The direct selector tests pass null pointers for all unused inputs and zero
charge/mass. Distinct prefilled output values verify the exact zeroed block,
preservation of all other entries, and zero CFL. This catches an accidental
return to ordinary geometry evaluation as well as an incorrect block size or
offset. These host selector tests are excluded in NVCC translation units,
where the selectors are device functions.

The public updater tests use both an axis cylinder and a mapc2p annulus. The
axis fixture explicitly verifies zero DG Jacobian and radial face area.
Mixed BCs set lower x, upper y, and lower z to zero flux. On the annulus,
all other output slots are compared to a reference with ordinary boundaries,
including untouched ghost slots and parallel-velocity flux. Both domains
check finite output and nonnegative finite cell CFL, and require that some
ordinary flux remains nonzero. Finiteness uses bit inspection so fast-math
cannot optimize away the checks. CUDA variants are registered when enabled
and compare against CPU reference output, including axis CFL.

Completed CPU checks on 2026-10-20:

- Library build and all five new unit test cases passed.
- Existing `ctest_gk_geometry_cylindrical`,
  `ctest_fem_poisson_perp_cylindrical`, `ctest_gk_geometry_mapc2p`, and
  `ctest_fem_poisson_perp` passed.
- Axis and annular LAPD regressions each completed two update calls with
  `-s 2 -x 4 -y 8 -z 2 -u 4 -v 2`. These are smoke tests, not convergence
  studies. Both reported RK stage-2 time-step retries and completed normally.
- Generator reproducibility, copied-file identity, and whitespace checks passed.

CUDA hardware/toolchain, Compute Sanitizer, and Valgrind are unavailable in
this environment. CUDA tests were added but not compiled or executed here;
no GPU or memory-sanitizer verification is claimed. R2–R4 and the broader
axis convergence/conservation checks remain separate work.
'''

# Instructions

* Use when working on the gyrokinetic/ code, or with an input file that uses
  the gyrokinetic solver.

# Gyrokinetics

## MPI decomposition

Gyrokinetic regression tests parallelize along the last configuration-space
dimension. Choose the partition flag by dimensionality:

| Dimensionality | Flag for N partitions |
|---|---|
| 1x2v | `-c N` |
| 2x2v | `-d N` |
| 3x2v | `-e N` |

For example, run the compiled 2x2v sheath regression on four MPI ranks:

```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 4 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -M -d 4
```

Use the MPI installation matching the build. `-M` enables MPI in the
regression executable; `-d 4` partitions its second configuration dimension.
Add `-s1` for a one-step smoke test.

See [compiling](../compiling/SKILL.md) when a build is needed,
and [testing-and-verification](../testing-and-verification/SKILL.md) for general test
execution and memory checks.

name: directory-structure
description: Locate Gkeyll code and understand solver dependencies when exploring the repository or deciding where new code belongs.
---

# Instructions

* Use when exploring the repository, trying to find something, or deciding where new code belongs.
* Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Gkeyll file structure

Gkeyll has four PDE solvers: 
* Moments or fluid solver.
* Vlasov solver.
* Gyrokinetic solver.
* PKPM solver.

Correspondingly, these solvers are organized into four separate folders, and they
share some common functionality in a fifth folder. Gkeyll is mostly organized in:
* core/: functionality common to all solvers.
* moments/: files for the moments solver.
* vlasov/: files for the Vlasov solver.
* gyrokinetic/: files for the gyrokinetic solver.
* pkpm/: files for the PKPM solver.

Note that the four solvers are not independent. They have the following
dependencies:
* moments depends on core.
* vlasov depends on moments.
* gyrokinetic depends on vlasov.
* pkpm depends on gyrokinetic.

Keep lower layers independent of higher layers.

Each of the solvers' folders have the sub-folders:
* ker/: C kernels generated with Maxima stored in the gkylcas repository. Do
  not hand-edit generated kernels; modify their source templates instead.
* zero/: C and CUDA functions or modules (sometimes we call them updaters),
  some of which call kernels in ker/.
* data/: data needed for some simulations.
* unit/: unit tests of specific components in zero/.
* apps/: apps are called by input files or regression tests, and they organize
  solver workflow or simulations and call modules in zero/. Communication
  happens in the app level.
* creg/: C regression tests or short simulations to ensure solvers work (these
  are also examples of C input files).
* luareg/: Lua regression tests or short simulations to ensure solvers work
  (these are also examples of Lua input files).

## Library dependencies

The Gkeyll source code in gkeyll/ depends on other libraries installed in gkylsoft/.
Most of the time you shouldn't need to read files in gkylsoft/ unless prompted.

## CPU - GPU organization

Gkeyll runs on both CPUs and GPUs, the latter using CUDA.
- CPU-only implementations live in .c files.
- C files call host-side wrappers of CUDA kernels, both of which live in _cu.cu
  files.

## Search hierarchy

Rather than looking into the entire codebase without prior knowledge, look into
folders in the following order:
- Look into a folder (ending in /) the user referenced.
- If the user referenced a specific solver (e.g. gyrokinetic), look into its
  folder.
- Look into folders for solvers that the specified solver depends on, following
  the dependency chain up through core/.

regression executable; `-d 4` partitions its second configuration dimension.

  The functions called in this file are in gkFuncs-alpha-surf.mac.
*/
load("gyrokinetic/gk_collisionless/gk_collisionless_flux-surf-conf.mac")$
load("gyrokinetic/gk_collisionless/gk_collisionless_flux-surf-vpar.mac")$

/* ...... USER INPUTS........ */

/* Serendipity basis. */
minPolyOrder_Ser : 1$
maxPolyOrder_Ser : 1$
minCdim_Ser : 1$
maxCdim_Ser : 3$

/* Tensor order basis. No need to generate p=1. */
minPolyOrder_Tensor : 2$
maxPolyOrder_Tensor : 2$
minCdim_Tensor : 1$
maxCdim_Tensor : 0$

/* ...... END OF USER INPUTS........ */

/* Vdim possibilities for each of Cdim=[1,2,3]. */
gkVdims : [[1,2], [2], [2]]$

/* To generate other bases, just add corresponding column to arrays below. */
bName        : ["ser", "tensor"]$
minPolyOrder : [minPolyOrder_Ser, minPolyOrder_Tensor]$
maxPolyOrder : [maxPolyOrder_Ser, maxPolyOrder_Tensor]$
minCdim      : [minCdim_Ser, minCdim_Tensor]$
maxCdim      : [maxCdim_Ser, maxCdim_Tensor]$

clabels : ["x","y","z"]$
vlabels : ["vpar","mu"]$

/* Options for writing kernels with and without toroidal field (b_y=0), one per
   dimension. */
byOpt : [[false], [false, true], [false, true]]$
byStr : ["", "no_by_"]$

/* Options for writing kernels used at multiblock boundaries. One for each
 dimension. */
mb_bcOpt : [[false,true],[false,true],[false,true]]$
mb_bcStr : ["", "multib_boundary_"]$

/* Generate kernels of selected types. */
for bInd : 1 thru length(bName) do (
  for c : minCdim[bInd] thru maxCdim[bInd] do (
    for gkV : 1 thru length(gkVdims[c]) do (
      v : gkVdims[c][gkV],

      maxPolyOrderB : maxPolyOrder[bInd],
      if (c=3) then maxPolyOrderB : 1, /* Only generate p=1 kernels for 3x2v */

      for polyOrder : minPolyOrder[bInd] thru maxPolyOrderB do (
        for byI : 1 thru length(byOpt[c]) do (
          no_by : byOpt[c][byI],
          no_byStr : byStr[byI],

          for mbI : 1 thru length(mb_bcOpt[c]) do (
            mb_bound : mb_bcOpt[c][mbI],
            mb_boundStr : mb_bcStr[mbI],

            /* Surface flux in direction dir in configuration space.*/
            for dir : 1 thru c do (

              fname : sconcat("~/max-out/gk_collisionless_flux_",no_byStr,mb_boundStr,"surf",clabels[dir],"_", c, "x", v, "v_", bName[bInd], "_p", polyOrder, ".c"),
              disp(printf(false,"Creating flux surf~a ~a ~a file: ~a",clabels[dir],no_byStr,mb_boundStr,fname)),

# Gyrokinetics

## MPI decomposition

Gyrokinetic regression tests parallelize along the last configuration-space
dimension. Choose the partition flag by dimensionality:

| Dimensionality | Flag for N partitions |
|---|---|
| 1x2v | `-c N` |
| 2x2v | `-d N` |
| 3x2v | `-e N` |

For example, run the compiled 2x2v sheath regression on four MPI ranks:

```sh
<mpi_install_prefix>/bin/mpirun -np 4 ./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 -M -d 4
```

Use the MPI installation matching the build. `-M` enables MPI in the
regression executable; `-d 4` partitions its second configuration dimension.
Add `-s1` for a one-step smoke test.

See [compiling](../compiling/SKILL.md) when a build is needed,
and [testing-and-verification](../testing-and-verification/SKILL.md) for general test
execution and memory checks.

# Instructions

* Use when exploring the repository, trying to find something, or deciding where new code belongs.
* Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Gkeyll file structure

Gkeyll has four PDE solvers: 
* Moments or fluid solver.
* Vlasov solver.
* Gyrokinetic solver.
* PKPM solver.

Correspondingly, these solvers are organized into four separate folders, and they
share some common functionality in a fifth folder. Gkeyll is mostly organized in:
* core/: functionality common to all solvers.
* moments/: files for the moments solver.
* vlasov/: files for the Vlasov solver.
* gyrokinetic/: files for the gyrokinetic solver.
* pkpm/: files for the PKPM solver.

Note that the four solvers are not independent. They have the following
dependencies:
* moments depends on core.
* vlasov depends on moments.
* gyrokinetic depends on vlasov.
* pkpm depends on gyrokinetic.

Keep lower layers independent of higher layers.

Each of the solvers' folders have the sub-folders:
* ker/: C kernels generated with Maxima stored in the gkylcas repository. Do
  not hand-edit generated kernels; modify their source templates instead.
* zero/: C and CUDA functions or modules (sometimes we call them updaters),
  some of which call kernels in ker/.
* data/: data needed for some simulations.
* unit/: unit tests of specific components in zero/.
* apps/: apps are called by input files or regression tests, and they organize
  solver workflow or simulations and call modules in zero/. Communication
  happens in the app level.
* creg/: C regression tests or short simulations to ensure solvers work (these
  are also examples of C input files).
* luareg/: Lua regression tests or short simulations to ensure solvers work
  (these are also examples of Lua input files).

## Library dependencies

The Gkeyll source code in gkeyll/ depends on other libraries installed in gkylsoft/.
Most of the time you shouldn't need to read files in gkylsoft/ unless prompted.

## CPU - GPU organization

Gkeyll runs on both CPUs and GPUs, the latter using CUDA.
- CPU-only implementations live in .c files.
- C files call host-side wrappers of CUDA kernels, both of which live in _cu.cu
  files.

## Search hierarchy

Rather than looking into the entire codebase without prior knowledge, look into
folders in the following order:
- Look into a folder (ending in /) the user referenced.
- If the user referenced a specific solver (e.g. gyrokinetic), look into its
  folder.
- Look into folders for solvers that the specified solver depends on, following
  the dependency chain up through core/.

# Instructions

* Limit your scope to the specific directory you are asked to work in, unless a
  dependency leads you to other directories or if there is ambiguity as to where new code should be
  placed (in which case you can ask the user).
* A small number of core kernels are generated using GINAC, see core/ginac,
  which requires ginac installation, see install-deps/.
* Operate relative to the repository root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# gkylcas file structure

gkylcas holds the computer algebra system (CAS) code to generate kernels used by Gkeyll. Gkeyll has
four PDE solvers: moments (fluid), Vlasov, gyrokinetic and PKPM. Correspondingly, these solvers are
organized into four separate folders, and they share some common functionality in a fifth (core)
folder. Hence, gkylcas is mostly organized in:
* core/: functionality common to all solvers.
* moments/: files for the moments solver.
* vlasov/: files for the Vlasov solver.
* gyrokinetic/: files for the gyrokinetic solver.
* pkpm/: files for the PKPM solver.

Note that the four solvers are not independent. They have the following
dependencies:
* moments depends on core.
* vlasov depends on moments.
* gyrokinetic depends on vlasov.
* pkpm depends on gyrokinetic.

There are other Maxima-specific utilities, independent of model or discretization, in util_maxima/.

name: software-design.
description: Consider established design practices when implementing new scripts or modifying existing ones.
---

# Instructions

* Follow existing software design, alert user when existing files don't adhere
  to such design, and suggest improvements to the design.
* When working with Maxima scripts, give preference to established approaches
  already in our codebase, but also suggest improvements based on other Maxima knowledge (for
  example what's in the Maxima documentation https://maxima.sourceforge.io/ext/maxima.pdf).

## Software design elements

### Module structure

Within each solver (e.g. core, gyrokinetic, etc), each there is (more or less) a separate folder
whose task it is to generate the kernels for a specific object or updater in Gkeyll (that is,
kernels for objects in Gkeyll's zero/ folders). Most of these gkylcas folders have two types of files:

1. A Maxima script to be run, whose name typically starts with ms-.
2. A file with functions called by ms- scripts.

In general the ms- scripts decide which kernels to generate for various dimensionalities, basis
types, and other varying properties.

### Module best practices

- The functions that ms- scripts call should have a `block([],` list in which
  all variables or local to the function should be listed. Failing to include private variables in
  this list can lead to memory leaks and erroneous results.

### Other principles to follow

- Consider extensibility, maintainability, simplicity and how modular design.
- Avoid code duplication whenever possible (e.g. write functions called
  multiple times) and without breaking layering.
- Write shorter code and refactor into a sub-module whenever possible.

### Variables

- In Maxima scripts, the _c suffix is typically used to indicate a list of DG

# Instructions

* Operate relative to the repo root (detect via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

# Code style

The style itself (indentation, brace placement, spacing, etc.) is defined by the
root `.clang-format` file plus one rule in `ci/format.py` (designated-initializer
layout, see below). Don't try to memorize or restate those rules -- just run the
formatter and let it decide:

```
python3 ci/format.py <file>...
```

Do not run bare `clang-format -i`: it packs designated initializers back onto one
line. `ci/format.py` needs clang-format 18.1.8 on PATH (`pip install clang-format==18.1.8`).

A `pre-commit` hook runs this automatically on commit, and CI (`.github/workflows/format-check.yml`)
double-checks on push/PR, so a file that hasn't been run through clang-format will
get reformatted or flagged regardless.

## The rules the config file can't express: never format `ker/` or `core/minus/`

Two kinds of files must never be run through clang-format, and never hand-formatted
to "match" the style either -- leave them exactly as they are:

- Any path matching `*/ker/*` (e.g. `core/ker/`, `gyrokinetic/ker/`) contains
  auto-generated DG kernel code (see `gkeyll_guide`'s note on `ker/`: generated with
  Maxima, never hand-edited).
- Anything under `core/minus/` is a vendored third-party library (e.g. sqlite3,
  kann, pcg_basic, STC), not Gkeyll's own code.

The pre-commit hook and CI already exclude both for this reason.

## Designated initializers: the script decides, not the trailing comma

A designated initializer that fits on one line stays on one line. One that does
not gets one member per line, first member below the `{`, closing `}` on its own
line. `ci/format.py` enforces this by stripping every trailing comma, running
clang-format, re-adding a trailing comma to each list that did not fit, and running
clang-format again. So don't add or remove trailing commas to steer the layout;
write the list any way you like and run the script.

## Two conventions the formatter enforces that you should know when reading code

- Every function *definition* has its return type on its own line, so
  `grep '^gkyl_foo('` finds the definition. Declarations keep the type on the same line.
- `case` labels are indented one level inside `switch`.

/* Both boundary edges and ES/NO_BY share a zero-flux kernel. The passive
   variant has the same flux layout but takes two prescribed-speed inputs. */
buildGKFluxConfZeroKernel(surfDir, fh, funcNm, cdim, vdim, basisFun, polyOrder, passive) := block(
  [varsC,bC,varsP,bP,vSub,surf_cvars,surf_vvars,numSurfNodes,offset,i],
  [varsC,bC,varsP,bP,vSub] : loadGkBasis(basisFun, cdim, vdim, polyOrder),
  surf_cvars : delete(varsP[surfDir],varsC),
  surf_vvars : makelist(varsP[i],i,cdim+1,cdim+vdim),
  /* Flux storage is nodal: p1 uses the gyrokinetic hybrid quadrature. */
  numSurfNodes : if polyOrder = 1 then length(gaussOrdGkHyb(2,surf_cvars,surf_vvars))
    else length(gaussOrd(polyOrder+1,cdim+vdim-1)),

  printf(fh, "GKYL_CU_DH double ~a(~%", funcNm),
  printf(fh, "  const double *w, const double *dxv,~%"),
  printf(fh, "  const double *vmap, const double *vmapSq, const double q_, const double m_,~%"),
  printf(fh, "  const struct gkyl_dg_surf_geom *dgs, const struct gkyl_gk_dg_surf_geom *gkdgs,~%"),
  printf(fh, "  const double *bmag, const double *jacobgeo_rat_surfL, const double *jacobgeo_rat_surfR,~%"),
  if passive then
    printf(fh, "  const double *speedsL, const double *speedsR,~%")
  else
    printf(fh, "  const double *phi,~%"),
  printf(fh, "  const double *JfL, const double *JfR, double *GKYL_RESTRICT flux_surf)"),
  printf(fh, "~%{~%"),
  printf(fh, "  // Zero only this direction's flux block. No geometry or input evaluation.~%"),
  for i : offset thru offset+numSurfNodes-1 do
    printf(fh, "  flux_surf[~a] = 0.0;~%",i),
  printf(fh, "  return 0.0; // No boundary CFL contribution.~%}~%")
